page.h1: HTS Chapter 30: Pharmaceutical Products — Foreign Tariff Changes on U.S. Exports

seo.title: Tariffs on U.S. Pharmaceutical Exports: What Changed Since 2025 (HTS Ch. 30) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Every tariff action since January 2025 that touched U.S. medicine exports: China’s retaliation (125% → 10%), Canada and EU counter-tariff lists, trade deals with the UK, Japan and Switzerland, and Brazil’s open reciprocity case.

intro: This page tracks what **other countries** changed on U.S. pharmaceuticals since January 2025 — retaliation, trade deals and removals — newest first. Only one measure actually costs U.S. medicine exporters money today: **China's extra 10%** on all U.S. goods. Canada's and the EU's counter-tariff lists left Chapter 30 out, and the 2025–26 deals with the UK, Japan, Switzerland and the EU did not need to cut tariffs that were already zero. For what the U.S. charges on imported medicines, see the import Tariff updates page.
scope: The 12 largest buyers of U.S. Chapter 30 goods (76% of 2025 exports). Measures on other U.S. goods are listed only where a buyer might reasonably expect them to reach medicines.

stats.label: Pending
stats.value: 2 (Brazil reciprocity, China Board of Trade list)

inEffect.measure: Extra tariff on all U.S. goods (State Council Tariff Commission)
inEffect.appliesTo: All Chapter 30 goods of U.S. origin, on top of China's 0–3% normal rate (5–10% on dressings and other 3006 goods).
inEffect.whatItMeans: A $1M shipment of U.S. antibodies pays about $130,000 instead of $30,000 at China's 3% normal rate. The extra rate peaked at 125% in April 2025; a further 24 points stay suspended under the truce to Jan 10, 2027.

changes.title: U.S.–China Board of Trade product lists
changes.detail: China’s list of 1,619 U.S. tariff lines that could get lower tariffs has only three Chapter 30 lines — adhesive dressings (3005.10.90), other wadding (3005.90.90) and dental/bone cements (3006.40). No vaccines, antibodies or packaged medicines.

changes.title: Counter-tariffs on U.S. products (answering U.S. Section 338 tariffs)
changes.detail: Mostly steel, aluminum, dairy, appliances, furniture and clothing. The list jumps from Chapter 19 to perfumes (3303), skipping pharmaceuticals entirely.

changes.title: Reciprocity process opened against new U.S. tariffs
changes.detail: Answers the 25% U.S. Section 301 tariff of July 2026. A 60-day consultation window ends around Oct 12, 2026. Options include higher tariffs on U.S. goods and, as a last resort, suspending intellectual-property rights such as pharmaceutical patents. No product list yet.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: U.S. declines to extend, annual reviews begin
changes.detail: Preferences continue for now; the agreement is reviewed every year instead of being renewed for 16 years. A future exit would expose U.S. goods to Mexican MFN rates.

changes.title: EU–U.S. framework tariff cuts adopted
changes.detail: The EU removes its tariffs on U.S. industrial goods under the August 2025 framework; U.S. medicines were already duty-free, so nothing changes for Chapter 30. On the U.S. side, the framework caps U.S. tariffs on EU pharmaceuticals at 15%.

changes.title: U.S.–UK pharmaceutical pricing arrangement
changes.status: In force; full text agreed Apr 2, 2026
changes.detail: Not a tariff: the UK raises the net price it pays for new medicines by about 25% and lifts NICE’s cost-effectiveness threshold, which should help U.S. drug sales. In return the U.S. exempts UK medicines from its Section 232 drug tariffs, subject to conditions.

changes.title: U.S.–Switzerland–Liechtenstein trade framework
changes.detail: Switzerland intends to apply zero duties on all U.S. industrial goods, including medicines. On the U.S. side, Swiss pharmaceuticals face at most 15% under the Section 232 drug tariffs.

changes.title: U.S.–Japan agreement
changes.detail: Japan committed to buy more U.S. farm goods and invest in the U.S.; no change to Japanese tariffs on medicines. On the U.S. side, Japanese pharmaceuticals face at most 15% under the U.S. Section 232 drug tariffs.

changes.title: Reciprocity review against the 50% U.S. tariff
changes.detail: Brazil began assessing countermeasures under its new Economic Reciprocity Law but imposed none.

changes.title: EU countermeasures on about €93B of U.S. goods
changes.detail: Reported to leave pharmaceuticals out (the line-level annex was not checked here). Suspended in August 2025 and, since July 2026, with no end date.

changes.title: Extra tariff on all U.S. goods cut to 10%
changes.status: In force; truce extended to Jan 10, 2027
changes.detail: Rose 34% → 84% → 125% in April 2025, then cut to 10% with 24 points suspended. In November 2025 China kept the 10% and extended the suspension for a year; the September 2026 truce runs to Jan 10, 2027. Applies to medicines on top of China’s normal rate.

changes.title: U.S.–UK Economic Prosperity Deal
changes.detail: UK concessions were a beef quota and a duty-free ethanol quota; UK tariffs on medicines were already zero.

changes.title: Reported exemptions for some U.S. medicines from the 125% tariff
changes.detail: Reuters reported that Chinese authorities privately told importers of some U.S.-made medicines, chips and aircraft engines that their goods were exempt. No list was published, so which drugs qualified is unverified.

changes.title: Announced retaliation against U.S. tariffs never applied
changes.detail: Mexico announced countermeasures in March 2025 but never published a list. Its January 2026 tariff increases on non-FTA countries do not apply to U.S. goods.

changes.title: 25% counter-tariff on C$30B of U.S. goods
changes.detail: The list jumped from silica sand (2505) to perfumes (3303); no pharmaceuticals. Canada repealed most of it on Sept 1, 2025, keeping only steel, aluminum and auto surtaxes.

byCountry.headline: U.S. medicines enter Germany duty-free, as everywhere in the EU, and no EU measure since 2025 has changed that. The 33% jump in 2025 sales is supply-chain driven, not tariff driven.
Duty-free. Much of what lands in the Netherlands is cleared there and then distributed across the EU, so this figure partly stands in for other EU buyers.

byCountry.tariffNow: Same + 10% extra on all U.S. goods
byCountry.headline: China is the only big buyer charging U.S. medicines more than in January 2025: an extra 10% on top of its 0–3% normal rate. It peaked at 125% in April 2025, when some U.S. drugs reportedly got quiet exemptions; sales dipped only 4%.
Japan charges nothing on U.S. medicines and did not retaliate. Only a few minor 3006 lines (e.g. lubricating gels, ostomy appliances) carry 2–4%. The 15% drop in 2025 sales is not tariff driven.
U.S. medicines enter Canada duty-free, and neither the 2025 nor the 2026 Canadian counter-tariff list included a single Chapter 30 line.
Duty-free. Belgium is a European vaccine and biologics hub, and U.S. sales there rose 45% in 2025 with no tariff change.
Duty-free. Unlike most EU buyers, Spain mainly takes finished packaged medicines from the U.S.
Duty-free. Ireland is also the largest supplier of U.S. pharmaceutical imports ($42.6B), so much of this trade is drug substance and biologics moving between plants of the same companies.
The UK charges nothing on U.S. medicines. The December 2025 pharma deal changed what the NHS pays for new medicines, not UK tariffs; the 36% drop in 2025 sales came before it.

U.S. medicines pay Brazil’s normal Mercosur rates — near zero for most biologics, around 10% on many packaged drugs. Brazil has not retaliated, but its August 2026 reciprocity case could; suspending drug patents is one listed option.
Duty-free. Switzerland abolished tariffs on all industrial goods in January 2024, and the November 2025 framework only locked that in for U.S. goods.
No Mexican tariff change has touched U.S. medicines; they still enter free under USMCA. Without USMCA they would face Mexico’s MFN rates (about 5% on many biologics).
